extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and mathematics students preparing seminar/colloquium/research talks (faculty, postdocs, graduate students)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative principles for preparing and delivering mathematics seminar/colloquium/research presentations, emphasizing clarity, timing, and audience adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare obsessively
rubrics_metrics.description: A 50-minute talk should be rehearsed end-to-end at least twice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rehearse the entire talk multiple times to ensure flow, timing, and clarity; practice reveals where explanations are weak or timing will run long.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for 45–50 minutes; running over 55 is rude. The audience's clock controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan to finish within the allotted time; cut material rather than risk running over. Respect audience schedules and conference/session constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-part repetition (tell them what you'll tell them, tell them, tell them what you told)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell the audience what you'll tell them, tell them, then tell them what you told.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the talk around a clear statement of goals, a development of those goals, and a brief summary/conclusion so the main message is heard and remembered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with a concrete example or motivating problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with a concrete example or motivating problem, not a definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with motivation or an example that illustrates the main idea; avoid leading with dry abstract definitions that lose non-specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the blackboard (or sparse handwritten/slide alternatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the blackboard, not slides (1974 advice; modern equivalent: handwritten tablet or sparse slides).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, present material progressively (e.g., on the blackboard) so the audience follows the development; if using slides, keep them sparse and hand-write or emulate board pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write large and organize the board
rubrics_metrics.description: Write large. Top of the board to bottom; left to right; never erase what is still in use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure all audience members can read what's written; arrange content so earlier needed material remains visible while you add new content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include at least one proof (or proof sketch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include some proof. Don't just announce theorems; show one proof — even a sketch — so the audience hears what makes the result possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate the mechanism or idea behind a result rather than only stating conclusions; choose a proof accessible to the audience level (full proof for specialists, sketch for general audiences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Skip routine technical details
rubrics_metrics.description: Skip the routine. Trust the audience to fill in standard manipulations; spend stage time on the hard idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit lengthy routine calculations or standard manipulations; focus live exposition on the novel or conceptually difficult steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect to known mathematics / motivate broader relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Connect to known mathematics. Place the result in the larger landscape; tell the audience why a non-specialist should care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give context, examples of related work, and reasons why the result matters beyond narrow technical interest; this helps non-specialists grasp importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't apologize or undermine the talk
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't apologize. Never say 'this won't be very interesting' or 'I don't have time to explain'. Cut the apologetic content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid self-deprecatory remarks or undercutting statements that lower the audience's expectations or distract from the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Face the audience; don't talk to the board
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't talk to the board. Face the audience; the back of your head does not enunciate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain eye contact and address listeners rather than turning your back; speak clearly and audibly to engage the room.

rubrics_metrics.name: One main idea per talk
rubrics_metrics.description: One main idea per talk. A talk is not a paper. Sacrifice everything to make the one idea clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus the entire presentation on communicating a single central message; cut auxiliary results and side projects if they distract from clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: End on time and keep the conclusion brief
rubrics_metrics.description: End on time, then stop. The conclusion is a brief summary plus a question — nothing more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclude with a concise summary and (optionally) a motivating question or open problem; avoid adding new material in the final minutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat Q&A as part of the talk
rubrics_metrics.description: Q&A is part of the talk. Repeat each question for the room before answering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate and prepare for questions; repeat or paraphrase audience questions so everyone can hear and so the answer is framed clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch the audience and adapt pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Watch the audience. When eyes glaze, slow down or back up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor listeners' reactions and adjust speed, level of detail, or re-explain points when comprehension appears to falter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reading slides aloud
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading the slides aloud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not simply read slide text to the audience; use slides as prompts or visual aids and explain in your own words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't stack definitions before motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Stacking definitions before any motivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce motivation or examples before presenting a sequence of formal definitions to keep listeners engaged and oriented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid long introductory historical surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: Long introductory historical surveys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep historical background concise and relevant; lengthy history can bore or distract from the main idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't cite your own results too early
rubrics_metrics.description: Citing your own results in the first 10 minutes ('As I showed in 1962…').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid early self-references that presume specialist interest; present motivation and main idea first before detailed bibliographic claims about your prior work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure notation remains available and defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Using notation defined only on a slide that is no longer visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep crucial notation visible or reintroduce it when needed; avoid relying on ephemeral slides for definitions the audience must recall later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid symbol-heavy presentations without English explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbol-heavy slides with no English glue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement symbolic expressions with plain-language explanations to help non-specialists and maintain comprehensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid presenting detailed proofs that cannot be followed in real time
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed proofs that no one in the room can follow in real time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer proof sketches or key steps when full technical detail is too dense for a talk; provide references for full proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not run over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Running over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Again: plan and edit to ensure talk finishes on schedule; running late is disrespectful and harms the session.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt the talk to the specific audience
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is no such thing as a good talk in the abstract. There are only good talks for particular audiences."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor content, level of rigor, choice of examples, and amount of technical detail according to whether the audience is specialists, graduate students, or a general departmental colloquium.
